I've been re-thinking your proposed solution for safety regarding the derivable values in bc::settings. I came to the conclusion that if we use standard C++ encapsulation mechanisms we can get it all: safety and performance.

So we have non-derivable values upon which other (derivable) values depend. I would make both of them private members and only make them accessible through getter methods. For the non-derivable values we'd then implement setter methods that will also update the dependent values. Consequently, the derivation of the values would be an one-off computation rather than recurring for each use.

This implementation would still be compatible with boost::program_options because the bc::settings setter methods can be passed into the boost::program_options's
notifer

method which then causes the value to be set according to the configuration.

The only drawback would be that bc::settings would not be perfectly consistent with the other settings classes. But with the current solution it's not either.

no you're missing my point - it is the responsibility of a storage device (e.g. SSD) to keep its data store in integrity. Indeed it may not keep integrity.

A filesystem (e.g. ZFS) may add a checksumming layer to storage device access, so that reads will fail if its underlying disk data was corrupted.

In case of unexpected shutdowns in particular, self-validation to identify anything broken and rewind all affected, would make all sense - rather than for instance terminate and require administrator intervention which is LibBitcoin's current behavior.

I agree that it not is reasonable for software behavior to be coherent if persistent storage breaks, just like it not is reasonable for software behavior to be coherent if RAM or CPU break. However, unexpected shutdowns happen, and also a user may like to run self-checking logics - in particular given the fiat cost of SSD wear for rewriting the whole blockchain, and the time it takes to resync the blockchain from scratch, some self-validation would make sense. I don't follow LibBitcoin's database models very well yet so I don't understand yet what degree of complexity they are.
